name: True Myeloschisis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Neural Tube Defects

criteria.description: Presence of an open, unfused spinal cord with absence of overlying skin and meninges
MRI or ultrasound evidence of spinal cord malformation with exposed neural tissue
Congenital neurological deficits consistent with spinal cord exposure such as lower limb paralysis or sensory loss
Visible defect in the dorsal midline with absent skin covering the spinal cord

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria (open spinal cord, imaging confirmation, and neurological deficits) must be present
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by imaging; genetic testing is not diagnostic but may be used to rule out syndromic associations.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Exposed, unfused spinal cord without skin covering
searchTerms: open spinal cord without skin cover

pathognomonic.symptomName: Absent deep tendon reflexes in lower extremities
searchTerms: missing deep tendon reflexes in legs

common.notes: Often associated with Arnold-Chiari II malformation

searchTerms: symptoms of tethered spinal cord later in life

occasional.symptomName: Skin ulceration or infection at lesion site
searchTerms: ulcers or infections on skin lesion
respiratory difficulties due to Chiari malformation

imaging: MRI showing open spinal cord defect with absent posterior vertebral elements
Ultrasound demonstrating exposed neural tissue in fetus or neonate
CT scan may show bony defects in vertebrae
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; multifactorial etiology including folate metabolism genes
other: Physical examination revealing open neural tube defect with exposed spinal cord
Neurological examination showing lower motor neuron signs below lesion

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of meningeal sac without exposed spinal cord
Spinal cord protrudes into meningeal sac covered by thin membrane
Partial skin coverage unlike true myeloschisis

redFlags: Visible open spinal cord defect at birth
Rapid neurological deterioration or infection at lesion site
Signs of increased intracranial pressure (e.g., bulging fontanelle, vomiting)
references: Moore KL, Persaud TVN. The Developing Human: Clinically Oriented Embryology. 11th ed. Elsevier; 2015.
Sadler TW. Langman’s Medical Embryology. 14th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019.
